The problem with focus in general is that it behaves differently whether or not the:

- browser is actually in focus
- the actual window of the frame is in focus
- or the dev tools are open

Because of this we normalized the focus behavior (or at least attempted to) with `cy.focused()`. When you call `cy.focus()` on an element that does not receive focus due to the above listed reasons - we not only normalize the event and fire all of the appropriate events but we keep track of the state of the 'focused' element internally. That enables us to then fire the proper 'blur' events when the element should have lost focus.

What we do is basically a polyfill for when the browser doesn't do the "right thing" just because its out of focus. 

I believe there was a specific technical reason we chose not to implement `have.focus` in the chai-jquery rewrite, but I can't remember what it was. 

The problem is that because we are normalizing focus it means Cypress is the only source of truth to understand what *should* be in focus even when its not. Because of that - the `have.focus` assertion would have to call into the Cypress machinery and could not use anything else. It would basically just be the same thing as the yielded result from `cy.focused()`.

We have some internal notes in the driver about exposing a new  configuration like: 
```
{ wrapDomElementsWithJQuery: false }
```

This would then prevent Cypress from *ever* wrapping any DOM elements it encounters in jquery - and instead pass everything along. Our internal command signatures would not change (they'd have to accommodate both object types) but when yielding the elements you'd need to update your code.

However I think this doesn't really solve your problem - it seems you probably want to *keep* the wrapping of jquery, but be able to lean into the native elements when you want to.

The problem is that Cypress will continually re-wrap DOM elements whenever they are returned as the subject of a command.  This is to ensure that internally Cypress always understands the type. It even converts jquery objects *from your application* back into our own. That's the only way we can control them deterministically.

If we didn't do that you could write this code:

```js
cy.get('element').invoke('get', 0).invoke('checkValidity')
```

The problem is that `invoke('get', 0)` will unroll the native DOM element but then it'll be wrapped back up when the next `invoke` runs.

I think currently it's not really that big of a deal to utilize a `then` or `should` to explicitly call what you're trying to do.

You cite that the command log is the problem here - that you cannot easily tell because its comparing booleans instead of objects. That would still be the case here with my example above. Chaining the `should` to the `invoke('checkValidity')` would still change the subject to be boolean and not DOM. So that wouldn't really help you.

Even in its current state the Command Log does in fact help provide visual reference for the assertion. Notice how the assertion is indented? It knows that the assertion is about the current subject: the `<input>`.

My final thought is that if you *did* want to assert in regards to something about the element then you'd need to add a chai assertion plugin. Something like `cy.get('input').should('be.valid'). You would then make that assertion do the right thing and could call whatever methods you like but keep the subject as the element reference.

That's exactly what we've done for all DOM based assertions here:

This is a pretty good start.

Couple things...

There are a bunch of built in stringifier functions in Cypress.

They do slightly different things and are used in a bunch of places in the driver...

```js
Cypress.utils.stringify(...)
Cypress.utils.stringifyArg(...)
Cypress.utils.stringifyActual(...)
```

The bigger problem with your custom command is that based on the way you've written this you've made it mostly impossible to retry assertions until they pass.

Why?

Well in the built in Cypress commands - each command has to decide **how** and if it should retry, and of course whether it has any built in default assertions.

There is an API for this but it has not been documented nor 100% formalized.

By returning the `cy.wrap` command at the very end - you're then passing off the `result` value to `cy.wrap` which then ends up utilizing the retry code built into that command.

That means that your assertions are actually chained to the `cy.wrap` and it will retry them until the pass.

The problem is that once you pass off an immutable value like a `Boolean` then retrying becomes worthless.

`cy.wrap` could not possibly do anything because its just been handed a value - it has no idea where it came from or anything.

I actually cannot think of a way to make this work using what you have available at the moment. We likely need to bite the bullet and document the retry API's.

Today I would just recommend looking at the driver code to see how `invoke` or `wrap` is created and then using those API's. We wrote them to be publicly available. You'll then have to implement your own retry logic. It's not that hard but you'll have to do some legwork.

However, this is not necessarily indicative of any kind of memory leak. The system task manager will not provide you a reliable means of calculating memory because of the way garbage collection works in the browser. Browsers will prime and hold onto object references way beyond whether or not they should be garbage collected. There is **no** way to force GC (without running Chrome in a specific mode). It's up to the browser to choose when and how it runs GC. 

To figure out a real memory usage you either need to use the Timeline Profiler which forces GC every 100ms or so. This mode will make Cypress tests run unimaginably slow which makes it somewhat difficult to use. The other option is to monitor the Chrome Task Manager.

You have to look at Javascript Memory - and more specifically the numbers in parenthesis. What this is distinguishing is **primed** memory as well as memory that's scheduled to be GC. You will see growth for each test that runs but then when you "rerun" the entire suite, it will drop back down temporarily before going back up again.

The real issue here is what I've described many times before. There is an entire proposal that goes into a lot of detail:  https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/issues/681#issue-259623204

It is simply this...

### You cannot use the GUI to run all of your tests.

That's the problem and the solution. You cannot run all of your tests. The GUI is a mode built specifically to run one or a small number of tests at a time.

Cypress is capturing snapshots of the DOM for every single command which uses up a massive amount of memory. Why does it do this? So you can debug your tests and application as you iterate on a single or small number of tests at a time. The GUI is not built to handle entire runs.

Currently you can tell Cypress to cleanup snapshots by setting the `{ numTestsKeptInMemory: 0 }` in `cypress.json`. This will purge snapshots aggressively but then you will lose the ability to debug any of your tests. 

If you want to run all your tests you need to do it from the command line using `cypress run`. In that mode it makes specific performance optimizations (like not taking snapshots) because it knows you're not iterating on a test or working with the results.

The problem is most definitely that the Windows site is not under your control and has employed security restrictions that prevent Cypress from working.

Visiting or interacting with 3rd party content is a common anti-pattern and the workaround is to always use `cy.request` for interacting with the party in order to isolate getting just the token part.

I think you are on the right track that you should just set the cookie / session stuff directly (and that will work). If you're being redirected by the client or server it's likely due to it **not** having the right session information to work. Perhaps the cookies are domain based cookies instead of host-only.

Check to see if Windows has a published SSO API that you can use directly with `cy.request`. I am sure they do. Use those API's and you'll avoid ever needing your UI to utilize their services - which insulates you from changes on their end. It'll also make testing much much faster.

Here's the anti pattern for reference.

https://docs.cypress.io/guides/references/best-practices.html#Visiting-External-Sites

Also please check out our SSO recipes that show this in action.

https://docs.cypress.io/examples/recipes/logging-in-recipe.html#Single-Sign-On

I'm going to close this issue as there is nothing that can be done on our part. We could deploy strategies to remove the javascript code causing Cypress to be redirected but even if we did there is a better approach and you shouldn't ever use the UI to accomplish this.

P.S. `chromeWebSecurity` is detailed in the following guide.

https://docs.cypress.io/guides/guides/web-security.html

All it does is remove cross origin restrictions. That's all it does. The host site can still deploy certain restrictions that prevent Cypress from working. These are all in `javascript` and it goes against our testing philosophy to try to bypass these. Whenever users come across these problems it is *always* indicative of a testing anti-pattern. Think of it as "good barriers".

**MY SECOND TRY ALLOWS ME TO VISIT UNLIMITED NUMBER OF DOMAINS!:**

First, you need to add Puppeteer to your project:

```
npm install puppeteer
```

Then you can use it like this:

**Parent test:**

```js
blahblahblah

cy.exec("node path\\to\\file.js --headed", {timeout: 180000})
        .then((result) => {
            console.log(result.stdout)
        })

blahblahblah
```

**Child test:**

```js
const puppeteer = require('puppeteer');

puppeteer.launch({headless: false, userDataDir: "./user_data"}).then(async browser => {
    const page = await browser.newPage();
    await page.goto('https://www.google.com');
    await page.waitFor('some_element');
    const message = await page.evaluate(() => document.querySelector('some_element').innerText)
    console.log(message)
    await browser.close();
  });

```
Important notes:

* If you run the code on Windows, DO NOT use anything other than CMD.exe to run Cypress, otherwise you will get an error:

https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/issues/789

* `console.log(message)` is used in child test to send data to STDOUT. It is then captured by `result.stdout `in parent test. You can also use STDERR to output the data (`console.error` instead of cypress.log in child test and `result.stderr `in parent test)

* Please keep in mind that when you run cy.exec(), your CWD (Current Working Directory) is the root of your Cypress repository, so in order to run any tests you need to use the relative path, like `cypress\\integration\\mytest.js`

* You can shorten the code to get the text from the element:

https://github.com/GoogleChrome/puppeteer/issues/3260#issuecomment-422081505

Instead of

```js
await page.evaluate(() => document.querySelector('#my-sweet-id').innerText)
await page.evaluate(() => document.querySelector('#my-sweet-id').innerHTML)
```

You can use page.$eval:

```js
await page.$eval('#my-sweet-id', e => e.innerText);
await page.$eval('#my-sweet-id', e => e.innerHTML);
```

ENJOY!

The root of the app is not cachable because of the MITM that Cypress performs (`document.domain = 'localhost'). 

This would make it (at least to me) that one would enable offline-mode *after* having started testing. First you'd want to install your service worker and such, adding all required files to the cache, and then run some tests. This would mean a global option is not required/desired - if you have no cache, no prior visits to the site - offline will never work anyways. 

## Design

```js
// Quick and dirty
cy.offline()
// - do tests inbetween
cy.online()

// A probably better way:
cy.network({offline: true})
// - do tests inbetween
cy.network({offline: false])
```

The latter would enable Cypress to at at later point also add throttling in the options. Not sure as to the usefulness of throttling, but that's point of discussion for another issue. 

## Docs

The Chrome Debugger (Chrome, Electron) allows for the following, but Firefox does not. 

```js
    Cypress.automation('remote:debugger:protocol', {
        command: 'Network.enable',
      })

      Cypress.automation('remote:debugger:protocol', {
        command: 'Network.emulateNetworkConditions',
        params: {
          offline: options.offline,
          'latency': 0,
          'downloadThroughput': 0,
          'uploadThroughput': 0,
          'connectionType': 'none',
        },
      })
```

## Hurdles

> @brian-mann wrote:
> If we did use Chrome's APIs to achieve this, it would essentially break Cypress's ability to do automation since websocket events would no longer be able to reach the server. So if we did tap into Chrome we could only partially throttle and not fully force into offline mode. Another option would be to use the WebRequest API's and whitelist Cypress network traffic but throttle or reject others.

Half-way through my test (within a single `it`), I was able to enable offline-mode without any problems (manually, that is). After the tasks have been queued at the start, there should not be any issues with that. 

## Update

I've created a PR, but I'm not making any progress on Firefox.

According to [this issue](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1553849) Firefox does not seem to implement `Network.emulateNetworkConditions` yet - and I haven't found a suitable replacement either. For some reason, those APIs don't have easily accessible documentation. 

The Firefox UI has a `Work offline` mode, which does the same - I just haven't found a way to automate this. 

## Update 2

Unless we figure out how to automate it for Firefox, the chances of any PR making it into Cypress are slim to none. 

Call to everyone: feel free to try and find a way ;-). 

## Update 3

Work on the `Network.emulateNetworkConditions` CDP command in Firefox has started. All seems to be going well, except that Firefox - as of writing- , [allows access](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1140284#c23) to everything that resolves to `localhost` even in `Work Offline`-mode. This is still being figured out to make automated testing a bit more useful.

- 📁 cypress
 - 📁 integration

- 📁 src
- 📄 package.json
- 📄 cypress.json

@tylergets I actually tried that and spent a lot of time setting it up a bunch of different ways (including [this suggestion](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/issues/95#issuecomment-588979939) and permutations blending different solutions) hoping for a different outcome. Whether I was using `fetch` (i.e. I did nothing) or `unfetch`, mocking the map style load and the map data wouldn't work. Only when I removed `fetch` completely was the map able to load fully, but of course, that broke GraphQL.

The error I was getting from the map was [`Style not done loading`](https://github.com/mapbox/mapbox-gl-js/issues/2268), which showed whether I used `fetch` or `unfetch` and not when I did `window.fetch = null`. My "solution" was to hook up a handler for `'style.load'` mentioned in [a comment](https://github.com/mapbox/mapbox-gl-js/issues/2268#issuecomment-401979967) to prevent rendering layers, knowing that without my style load mock, the style never loads.

```js
    cy.visit("/")
      .wait("@query")
      .wait("@query")
      .wait("@query")
      .wait("@query")
      .wait("@query")
```

It also worked for us in a chained then()

```js
    cy.visit("/").then(()=> {
      cy.wait("@query")
      cy.wait("@query")
      cy.wait("@query")
      cy.wait("@query")
      cy.wait("@query")
   }
```

I had the same issue, locally all is working fine but on GitLab CI, one or two tests always fail with the above mentioned error message: `Error: ESOCKETTIMEDOUT`.

Currently, I workaround this by using [`cypress-plugin-retries`](https://github.com/Bkucera/cypress-plugin-retries), so when the error happens, the test gets retried.

Unfortunately I can't tell you how to reprocedure the whole thing, because it very sporadically always hits different tests. But basically it happens at `cy.visit()`. Previously I used `cypress@3.8.4` and never got this error before. I read more about it in GitHub issues and perhaps this is another "workaround": https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/issues/350#issuecomment-267704772; but I did not test it.

Similar tickets: #6547, #5975
Used Cypress Version: 4.4.1

The issue specifically reappeared after latest update to 4.4.1, is there any change that could have affected this? Will try to produce a repro later.
Edit: adding `cypress` to excluded folders of my global `tsconfig` did the job. But I am not sure why the issue appeared suddenly, there might be an underlying root cause.

If you stub the `window.navigator` to `cookieEnabled: false`, then this will mock visiting the application as if you do not have cookies enabled. This is expected behavior. If you don't have cookies enabled then Amazon shows a warning telling you cookies are not enabled. 

Also, we very strongly encourage you to not test website that are not under your control. So, unless you are a developer at Amazon, you should not be using Cypress to test Amazon sites. https://on.cypress.io/best-practices#Visiting-external-sites

This is the default behavior of the `its()` command as explained here: https://on.cypress.io/its#Assertions

We don't really intelligently look at what you passed to `its()`, so it's assumed that the state could change (which is the case for objects on the application for example). 

We could be smarter about this when the `its` is being passed an alias from a `cy.wait()` command.

### Workaround

You can get around this by setting a very low `timeout` option within the `its()` when you know the object it's asserting on cannot change after it exists. 

```js
cy.wait('@saveUser').its('request.body', { timeout: 0 }).should('deep.equal', editUserRequest);
```

It doesn't look like this `timeout` option is documented for `its()` so I'll need to update the docs for that. 

### Reproducible Example

```js
it('test', () => {
  cy.visit('http://example.cypress.io/commands/network-requests')
  cy.server()
  cy.route('GET', 'comments/*').as('getComment')
  cy.get('.network-btn').click()
  cy.wait('@getComment').its('status').should('eq', 404)
})
```

Hello Chris. I’m finally coming back to this. My understanding is that it makes a big difference, because what you receive in 4.2.0 is an object — correct me if I’m wrong. That means you can read its keys, its values, and so on. In 4.3.0 however, the received `error` is a string. Which means it’s not possible to access only `error.message`, or `error.name` or `error.stack`, making it not so useful anymore.

You still receive an object with `message`, `name`, and `stack` in either version. That can be seen in your original screenshot of the stdout. It prints an object with those properties.

The difference is that `error.message` is a `String` instance instead of a primitive string. But it behaves the same as a string. It has a `length` property and if you print it by itself, it will look the same.

I understand that Cypress wants to be fast. But it in this case it does not make a sense.

**1. Type checks are the reason why use TypeScript**.
2. I expect that Cypress also uses _tsc_ to compile my _.ts_ files. There is no reason to compile it again with another webpack and tsc. In the result...it would be much slower then the previous solution, when we used just webpack preprocessor and tsc....
3. It should be developer's  decision what restrictons are used. 
4. I need to see errors from compiler. IDE like VS Code is not enough. If I make a change in one file and it creates an error with some restrictions, which will have impact in another file, then I would not know about it, because IDE just shows errors in opened files. And to be honest... you can also simply dismiss errors from IDE. It is like you don't have TypeScript.

Consider this as a bug, not as a feature, because embedded TypeScript whithout type checks I defined in tsconfig.json is not usable. It has no sense and I still have to setup webpack preprocessor, so finally compile it twice...

1\. I agree type checks are the reason why we use TypeScript. But tsc can do the job. Cypress doesn't have to do it again. 
2\. Cypress doesn't use `tsc`. It uses [TypeScript compiler API](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/Using-the-Compiler-API#a-simple-transform-function). And Cypress should bundle its own runner program together with your test code. So, we cannot simply use the code built with your webpack settings. 
3\. Yes, you're right. Tools should give developers to choose their own restrictions. That's why you can use [cypress-webpack-preprocessor](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress-webpack-preprocessor) or [cypress-browserify-preprocessor](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress-browserify-preprocessor) to control the Cypress preprocessing process. 
4\. To restrict everyone to obey types, I guess the better way is to use `tsc --noEmit` and add it to your CI to check it every time you push something to your repo.

Yeah, I can confirm this behavior.

### Why

So, what I've discovered is happening here is that we seem to have patched *one* of the lodash methods with [underscore.string](https://gabceb.github.io/underscore.string.site) methods. 

I can't find the exact git blame, since it spans across old repos, but I'm 95% sure that this comment is from @brian-mann about the use of overriding lodash capitalize with `underscore.capitalize`:

```
// its mo' better the lodash version
```

https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/blob/develop/packages/driver/src/config/lodash.js#L11:L11

This appears to be the **only** lodash method we are overriding (although we added some new methods from underscore.string).

I think this is completely unexpected behavior, especially since this is not documented anywhere. I'll have to discuss with the team how to handle this - if this would be considered a breaking change or a 'fix' to change. 

### To Reproduce

`package.json`

```json
{
  "devDependencies": {
    "cypress": "4.5.0",
    "lodash": "^4.17.15",
    "underscore.string": "^3.3.5"
  }
}
```

`spec.js`

```js
const lodash_ = require('lodash')
const underscoreString_ = require('underscore.string')

it('works', () => {
  expect(lodash_.capitalize('FOO BAR')).to.eq('Foo bar')           // passes
  expect(underscoreString_.capitalize('FOO BAR')).to.eq('FOO BAR') // passes
  expect(Cypress._.capitalize('FOO BAR')).to.eq('FOO BAR')         // passes
})
```

Here is what is going on, and I do not consider this a bug, just the way bundling happens. You can find the supporting code in https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress-test-tiny/commit/08172373ff30d0e78544cc240c0a88155ecf035f Anything bundled from the support file gets its own bundle. Anything imported from the spec file gets into _second_ bundle. These two bundles are served for the spec If you open the `support` bundle you will see the `Username` object from "globals" If you open the spec bundle you will ALSO see the `Username` object` from "globals" Each bundle has its own copy of "Username" imported from the file, changing a property in one does not change it in the other. If you want to share data and object references between the support bundle nd the spec bundle, do it through the `window` object. ```js // support file import { Username } from './globals' window.Username = Username Cypress.Commands.add('printName', () => { console.log('command globals name: %s', Username.name) }) ``` ```js // spec file const Username = window.Username describe('globals', () => { it('shows username', () => { console.log('in spec username is "%s"', Username.name) console.log('now changed it to "foo"') Username.name = 'foo' console.log('in spec username is "%s"', Username.name) cy.printName() }) }) ```

I managed to build a multi-upload command based on this input, which takes an array of fixture-paths and names and upload multiple files in a single array.

In case anyone needs it:
 ```js
Cypress.Commands.add('uploadMultiple', ({localPaths = [], fileNames = [], mimeType = 'image/png'}) => {
  const fixtures = (paths) => Promise.all(paths.map(p => cy.fixture(p)))
  const encoding = 'base64'

  fixtures(localPaths).then(filesContents => {
    const payload = fileNames.map((fileName, i) => (
      {
        fileContent: filesContents[i],
        fileName,
        encoding,
        mimeType
      }))
    cy.get('input[multiple]')
    .upload(payload) 
  })
})
 ```

In regards to `error_messages.js`, I think it's less than ideal that  has to be left-aligned in order to get the proper whitespace. That’s an area where CoffeeScript is superior because it allows you to indent to align with the code, but strips out unnecessary whitespace in an intuitive way.

I wonder if we can pass these strings to a function or use a tagged template for them that can do something similar. Since tagged templates don’t have CoffeeScript’s benefit of being executed at compile-time, they can’t know the correct level of indentation to strip. I think we might need to just use a function and pass in the level of indentation, which isn’t the best, but it’s better than left-aligning everything in my opinion.

So it might look something like:

```javascript
{
  command: {
    some_error: s(3, `
      You made a grievous error.

      I can't believe you've done this.
    `)
  }
}
```

We pass `3` because it’s 3 levels of indentation (6 spaces) in. It can also strip the opening and closing newline and extra whitespace, so we don’t need the backslashes, and the string ends up like this:

This is happening because you're constructing the RegExp in the Test Runner window (which is a different window than your application under test window) - `instanceof` will only look at the host object that created it, since they’re 2 different windows it will be false. It’s the exact same behavior that would happen when having an iframe within another window frame - `instanceof` won’t work for this check. 

This is why instanceof is not the best way to do type detection. I'd recommend using lodash or a method similar to what they use to detect the type of the value. http://tobyho.com/2011/01/28/checking-types-in-javascript/ (across windows behavior is explained in `Cross-window Issues of instanceof` section)

If any of the others happen (except EPIPE, I'm not entirely sure on that one), then the client has a guarantee that the server did not receive the request, and thus it's safe to retry, but ECONNRESET (and potentially EPIPE) seem to me like they don't fit that pattern.

As a workaround we use a script and manually list all the test we want to use:

```sh
  cypress run --spec="cypress/integration/test1.js" &&
  cypress run --spec="cypress/integration/test2.js" &&
  cypress run --spec="cypress/integration/test3.js" 
  exit $? # in case this is not the end of your script because you are in a "if" or something

```javascript
cy.wait("@updateAttachment", {responseTimeout: 15000});
```

makes it sound like the request was never fired after the wait() call. In fact, the request did not finish before the 5000ms, that's why it failed. Adding a greater responseTimeout solved my issue.

`The cypress npm package is installed, but the Cypress binary is missing.
 We expected the binary to be installed here: /home/circleci/.cache/Cypress/3.5.0/Cypress/Cypress`

The solution was to persist the `cypress/*` folder:
```
- persist_to_workspace:
    root: .
    paths:
      - node_modules/*
      - cypress/*
```

I can't speak to how junit creates their reports.

Our web application is an Intake form for incidents.
When the user enters (manually) an address and Enters, the app sends a request to a geoserver to get a location (x,y).
Example: http://ourserver/arcgisproxy/rest/services/Utilities/Geometry/GeometryServer/project/... (this is a GET request).
This works fine, there is no request header "proxy-connection" in the request.

When we run our Cypress E2E test, the test fills in the address. Then our web application sends the request to the geo server.
In that situation, there is a request header "proxy-connection" in the request. And then the geo server fails.

Further prove: when we take the URL and post it in any browser's search box, we get a correct response.
When we post the same URL in a browser opened by Cypress, the request fails because it has the "proxy-connection" header.

So our conclusion is that Cypress adds the "proxy-connection" header.

Note:
We have made a test in Cypress:
when we run cy.request('our request') the request is succesfull.
when we run the same request using an XMLHttpRequest() the request has the "proxy-connection" header and fails.

So, although you say "The only time we manually insert "proxy-connection: keep-alive" is when the initial request contained "proxy-connection: keep-alive"",
it seems that some-one is setting this header?

Quick update:

- `Network.emulateNetworkConditions` has landed in Firefox 78.0a1 nightly (around 4:00 UTC this morning) :tada: 
- Firefox [always allows requests to `localhost`](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1634246), as well as anything that resolves to it - even in offline mode (no patch in progress yet)
- I've managed to enable CDP for Firefox in Cypress, but this required two more changes:
    - `Browser.getVersion` update in Firefox (patch added and landed in 78.0a1)
    - `Network.getAllCookies` support in Firefox (patch added, and accepted)

With all of the above patches in Firefox, I've managed to successfully implement `cy.network` on Firefox as well. Offline-only, so no throttling etc., but hey - that's all this issue is about. 

Regarding Chrome there's still the issue of service-workers ignoring offline emulation, but for the past two weeks others have been working hard on Chrome to fix [that issue](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1068544) as well - so I'm not worrying about that, that just means that service-worker support is only for newer Chrome versions. > I ask because this comment seems to imply that caching DOES work, but it is in-memory, not written to disk.

Quick peek into chromium source code shows that this behavior (cache not work with invalid cert) is intended and cannot be prevented with browser arguments: [/net/http/http_cache_transaction.cc](https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/55f44515cd0b9e7739b434d1c62f4b7e321cd530/net/http/http_cache_transaction.cc#L3096)

Anyway, I have made a quick test:

Chrome 81
Windows 10
Cypress 4.5.0

1) invalid certificate = **no caching**

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5988563/81989032-c83f0980-963c-11ea-9007-5a8a78575117.png)

2) trusted certificate = **caching works as expected**

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5988563/81989268-3b488000-963d-11ea-9946-b69a6ff6b509.png)

Our application leverages http caching for some quite heavy REST API calls and since I have rewritten some of our e2e tests from Selenium to Cypress, I have immediately noticed that Cypress test cases run much slower than those running via Selenium.

> It would be a security issue too. Although the test runner's CA keys are not shared pubicly (they are generated locally per-computer and cached), it's possible that malware on a user's computer could read the CA file and use it to intercept HTTPS traffic without the user's knowledge (if Cypress were added to the CA store)

I'm not really familiar with internal working of those certificates and theirs potential security issues but we could perhaps inspire at .NET Core SDK that provides a CLI option to make its own development certificate trusted [Trust the ASP.NET Core HTTPS development certificate on Windows and macOS](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/security/enforcing-ssl?view=aspnetcore-3.1&tabs=visual-studio#trust-the-aspnet-core-https-development-certificate-on-windows-and-macos) and in addition, we could inform users about the potential security risk you mentioned.

The cause of the CI failure is the folder structure.

```
root/cypress
- node_modules
  - @types/mocha
- test-cypress-and-jest
  - node_modules
    - @types/jest
```

By default, typescript tries to load all `node_modules/@types` from the project and its parent folders. And in CI, we used root/cypress to build cypress and we downloaded `@types/mocha` in the folder. That's why this happened.

The solution to make it pass is to reorganize the folder structure.

I tried to fix it on #7359, but for some reason, `test-cypress-and-jest` is not executed in my PR. So, I closed it and left a review.

@EtienneBruines From https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/NavigatorOnLine/onLine, it sounds like all browsers return `true` for `navigator.onLine` if the OS has any active network connection, regardless if they truly have access to the Internet or not. 

Since the browser will still be able to see the OS's network connection regardless of what the proxy layer is doing in #4176, I'm assuming #4176  will not affect `navigator.onLine`.

The HTML spec is pretty candid about this point: 

> This attribute [navigator.onLine] is inherently unreliable. A computer can be connected to a network without having Internet access.
> — https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/offline.html#navigator.online

git bisect start v3.8.0 v3.7.0 --

`test.sh` content:
```bash
#!/bin/bash

# Source: https://stackoverflow.com/a/49412454/305436

  perl -e "{if($1>$2){print 1} else {print 0}}"
}

COMMAND="yarn dev --run-project my-tests --spec '**/tests/loop.js'"
DURATION_LIMIT=30

yarn

# Source: https://stackoverflow.com/a/26785328/305436

if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then

  exit 125
fi
exec 3>&- 4>&-

if [ $(float_gt $DURATION $DURATION_LIMIT) == 1 ]; then
  echo "Took too long: $DURATION"
  exit 1
fi

echo "Fast enough: $DURATION"

> However, in both cases the casted value will be in the assertion failure message - leading the user to then fix it.

I don't know, it feels like a big assumption that this will be an improvement to the user experience. I feel like this will be the user story if this change goes in as-is:

1. User has a 16-digit credit card field on their site and wants to fill it in. (common use case) `cy.get('.cc').type('9999999999999999')`
2. User wants to assert that some specially formatted field contains the text '9999999999999999'.
3. User types `cy.get('.cc').should('have.text', 9999999999999999)`
4. `9999999999999999` is over the int limit so it is internally converted to `10000000000000000`.
5. Assertion fails with "Error: expected .cc to contain 9999999999999999 but really contained 10000000000000000"
6. Now the user is confused... they do one of the following:
	* They open a bug report, stating that "assertions are comparing the wrong numbers", then we point them to this issue and tell them to wrap their expected value in quotes
	* They try changing their test value to a different value, eg `1111111111111111` ( this is NOT over the int limit, so it will *work*) User goes "huh, weird, why does it work now?" and either opens up a bug report stating "assertions fail if i use 16 9's but succeed if i use 16 1's" or doesn't open up an issue at all and just thinks Cypress is bad at math
	* They happen to have a good knowledge of Javascript and where the integer-float boundary lies and so they intuitively understand that "Error: expected .cc to contain 9999999999999999 but really contained 10000000000000000" can be fixed by setting the expected value as a string, not a number

I think for a significant % of people who run into this issue, the solution will be non-obvious. Compare to the user story if we throw an error up front: 

1. User has a 16-digit credit card field on their site and wants to fill it in. `cy.get('.cc').type('9999999999999999')`
2. User wants to assert that some specially formatted field contains the text '9999999999999999'.
3. User types `cy.get('.cc').should('have.text', 9999999999999999)`
4. Assertion fails with "Error: have.text assertions expect a string as a parameter to match against, but a number was passed instead"
5. User understands that they did not pass a string and changes spec code to expect a string. Test passes.

I get what you mean, users are probably unlikely to run into this bug... but once they do, it will become very confusing very quickly. :shrug:

Cypress automatically waits for the element to meet the expectations your chained to its assertion. So there's no need to tell it to 'wait', it's automatic. 
I suggest reading the entirety of our [Introduction to Cypress]

(https://on.cypress.io/introduction-to-cypress) guide and our guide on built in [retry-ability](https://on.cypress.io/retry-ability)

To wait for an element to disappear, for example, you would write the code below, which will wait 4 seconds for the element to not be visible:

```js
cy.get('div').should('not.be.visible')
// or whatever your assertion is
cy.get('div').should('have.css', 'display', 'none')
```

You can increase the time Cypress waits by passing a larger timeout.

```js
cy.get('div', { timeout: 10000 }).should('not.be.visible')
```

There's also some dom utilities to check for these things you might find useful: https://on.cypress.io/dom

### User Experience

- The feature/bugfix is self-documenting from within the product.
- The change provides the end user with a way to fix their problem (no dead ends).

### Functionality

- The code works and performs its intended function with the correct logic.
- Performance has been factored in (for example, the code cleans up after itself to not cause memory leaks).
- The code guards against edge cases and invalid input and has tests to cover it.

### Maintainability

- The code is readable (too many nested 'if's are a bad sign).

- There are comments containing link(s) to the addressed issue (in tests and code).

### Quality

- The change does not reimplement code.
- There's not a module from the ecosystem that should be used instead.
- There is no redundant or duplicate code.
- There are no irrelevant comments left in the code.
- Tests are testing the code’s intended functionality in the best way possible.

The code above would trigger the code after every single **command** has run. A command is something like `cy.get()`, `.click()`, not after the entire Cypress run has completed. This event yields a command, not a test, so will not have a state of failed or passed as a test does. 

If you want to run some code after each test execution, I would recommend calling a [`cy.task()`](https://on.cypress.io/task) from within an `afterEach` hook that will call into the code you want to execute. All code within the event handlers or tests will have to be run within the context of the browser, so running code that needs to run in Node needs to be done in a `cy.task()`.

If you want to run some code after the Cypress run has finished, I recommend using our [Module API](https://on.cypress.io/module-api) which will return the full results of a run, including an array of tests that would include failed tests. 

Also, check out our [community chat](https://on.cypress.io/chat), it can be helpful for debugging or answering questions on how to use Cypress.

Alright, after looking through the commits in https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/pull/6522, I've further narrowed down the issue to the changed made in the `packages/runner`.

Specifically the upgrade of `react-dom` from `16.8.6` to `16.12.0`. If you downgrade this in the current `develop` of Cypress, you'll see this issue no longer occurs. 

It seems this was a bug in `react-dom` actually introduced in [`16.9.0`](https://github.com/facebook/react/releases/tag/v16.9.0) and not fixed in their current version of React (Although I’m inclined to think it’s likely [a Chromium bug that is not playing nicely with React](https://github.com/facebook/react/issues/16087)).

The way you've written the tests makes is non-deterministic when the translator request will go out, so if they go out before the cy.route() is run in the `beforeEach`, then they won't be stubbed - as you've explained. You'll need to write your tests in a more deterministic way. 

- Writing explicit waits as you've seen is a great example of determinism - you want to make sure your test steps don't continue until this request has responded. 
- We would also not recommend visiting the site once, but visiting `beforeEach` test so that state from the previous test doesn't leak into the next test and affect it in unexpected ways.
- There's no determination on when the 'dummy' test should run also, so it's a matter of timing where you're app loading will be by the time it is run, normally  you would define some sort of state for 'my app is loaded', so that the next test doesn't run before then. 
- We also wouldn't recommend [relying on the state of previous tests for next tests](https://docs.cypress.io/guides/references/best-practices.html#Having-tests-rely-on-the-state-of-previous-tests).

This is because you've added a command with the name 'reset', which is a reserved word that Cypress uses as an internal command. This is not documented anywhere however.

The `before` is further swallowing up the error for some reason, but you can see some kind of error in the console, albeit wouldn't lead you to understand that `reset` is reserved for command names. 

https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/blob/develop/packages/driver/src/cypress.js#L364:L364

```js
Cypress.Commands.add('reset', () => {})

describe('tests', () => {
  before(() => {})

  it('test', () => {
    expect(true).to.be.true
  })
})
```

## Workaround

Rename your custom command anything other than `reset`. 

```js
Cypress.Commands.add('resetApp', () => {}) // works now!
```

Closing this as a duplicate of https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/issues/6146 which documents another reserved word for commands that someone else encountered.

@Brestachan We encountered similar issue in our application.

Depending on the way you are handling authentication, this might be your problem as well.

If the Cypress browser has an invalid certificate, any cookies with the `secure` flag will not work. 

So, lets say you hit an endpoint `/login` in order to log in, and the server that handles that endpoint sends back a Set-Cookie Response Header, which writes the authentication cookie to the browser. 

If the Set-Cookie header includes the `secure` flag and you are not using https or possibly have invalid certificates, the cookie will not be written to the browser, so its almost as if you never logged in at all ( you can inspect the browser cookies and you will see that the authentication one is not there ).

This becomes prominent when the page is refreshed - you will not be logged in, because the browser does not have the cookie in it. However, once you log in, if you don't refresh, you are actually browsing as a logged in user.

I suspect that `axios` ( which is what I am using ) reads the `Set-Cookie` Response Header and manually attaches it to further requests, which is why it would work until you have reloaded the page.

At least half of this is theory, so don't get too attached to it. The root cause, I'm assuming, would be the invalid SSL certificate.

While this work is ongoing, and yet to become part of Cypress officially, here's some steps for folks that might want to try building the modified 6.6.0 source as currently on this fork, and running cypress that way. Bear in mind this is development code still, it should work fine, but YMMV, caveat emptor and all that!

Note: These instructions assume you have cloned the appropriate cypress source repo, and have yarn installed

1. Build
Install dependencies:
    ```
    yarn
    ```
    
Now build the binaries for the required target OS - Note!! Requires that the build agent has the same OS! When prompted, choose to just override the currently deployed version.
```
yarn binary-build --platform=linux
```
or
```
yarn binary-build --platform=win32
```
Finally, produce a cypress.zip output:
```
yarn binary-zip
```
Installing
Update your test application to Cypress v6.6.0, this will install the Cypress binaries and the related JavaScript interface(s)
```
npm install --save-dev cypress@6.6.0
```
Remove the 6.6.0 binaries from the follow path as appropriate. Optionally, you can also specify the child 6.6.0 folder as appropriate to only remove the binaries for that version:
Linux: ~/.cache/Cypress
Windows: /AppData/Local/Cypress/Cache

Now install the newly created binaries (bash syntax shown - adapt as appropriate for your platform). Note that you'll need to copy the cypress.zip created above to the current folder for this step (or modify to specify an absolute path, not relative).
```
CYPRESS_INSTALL_BINARY=$(pwd)/cypress.zip npm install --save-dev cypress@6.6.0
```

@jennifer-shehane I think that's for the internal isolated runner. We want to set the retries for the internal isolated runner on a spec-by-spec basis (eg. so that retries can set it to non-zero) but the retries for the outer runner to remain at 0. Basically the "inner Cypress" - `createCypress({})` call should have `retries` set to whatever we're testing (`0` for most files, `2` for the retries spec) while the "outer Cypress" should have `retries` always set to 0 so that it never retries the snapshot comparison (eg. our top-level `describe` should have the config param with `retries: 0`).

The code for this is done in [cypress-io/cypress#15666](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/pull/15666), but has yet to be released.
We'll update this issue and reference the [changelog](https://on.cypress.io/changelog) when it's released.

As part of Cypress’s [new pricing](https://www.cypress.io/blog/2021/03/16/new-pricing-that-scales-seamlessly/), we’ve included the ability to [cancel test runs when a test fails](https://on.cypress.io/smart-orchestration#Cancel-test-run-when-a-test-fails). This setting is accessible from the Dashboard for organizations starting at the [Business Plan](https://www.cypress.io/pricing/).

This offers a possible solution for the situation outlined in this issue - for those running tests using the Cypress Dashboard - and also ensures a parallelized run is cancelled so that all parallel running specs will also be cancelled to save time on the run.

**To get this feature, you will need to update to Cypress 6.8.0 and also be a member of an organization subscribed to a [Business Plan](https://www.cypress.io/pricing/).**

---

This feature was implemented with parallelized runs in the Dashboard in mind since this was the hardest use case to address. We had to build this feature specifically to continue to receive all of the tests in a cancelled run to ensure proper reporting. Now that we have a mechanism to cancel runs across these channels of communication, we can now consider a way to initiate cancelling test runs when a test fails from the Test Runner when not recording to the Dashboard. (Likely this would be implemented by some CLI flag or config specifying `cancelOnFailures: true)

**This issue https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/issues/518 will remain open to address the use case of cancelling test runs when a test fails from the Test Runner when not recording to the Dashboard.**
I would recommend for visual regression testing that you use `--headless` when generating the screenshots. Otherwise it's nearly impossible to get consistent screenshots across OS/screen sizes.

This setting is accessible from the Dashboard for organizations starting at the [Business Plan](https://www.cypress.io/pricing/).

This offers a solution for those running tests using the Cypress Dashboard since the feature itself requires a history of runs (that have been recorded).

**To get this feature, you will need to update to Cypress 6.8.0+ and also be a member of an organization subscribed to a [Business Plan](https://www.cypress.io/pricing/).**

> ### Workaround
> Use `global.parent.Object` instead of `Object`.
> 
> ```js
> console.log('Cypress Fixture', fixture instanceof global.parent.Object) // => true
> ```
> 
> ### Why it happened?
> When `iframe`s are in the HTML code, there are multiple `Object`s which came from the `window`s. We need to check where it came from.
> 
> In Cypress, there are 3 types of windows:
> 
> 1. Runner: This contains everything. The reporter is on the left (the list of test names we all know and love). Cypress commands are run under this context.
> 2. App: The app under test on the right (where you can see how your app is working.)
> 3. Test file: It is not visible. Test files are run under the browser. It became possible because files is loaded into an iframe.
> 
> When we simply write `Object` on a test file, it's from 3, test file. And the parent `Object` of the object generated by `cy.fixture()` is from 1, the runner. That's why simple `fixture instanceof Object` didn't work.
> 
> ### Problem & Possible Solution
> It's super unintuitive.
> 
> Maybe, we need to create APIs like `cy.runner()` that returns the runner window like `cy.window()`. Then, we can rewrite the code like below:
> 
> ```js
> cy.runner().then(runner => {
>   console.log('Cypress Fixture', fixture instanceof runner.Object) // => true
> })
> ```

Unfortunately, that wouldn't work in this case. the Object check is in the app code, not spec code.

Hi @tannera,

I have some updates on this request.

Firstly, we just released Cypress 7.0, which comes with a completely revamped Component Testing experience. Component testing is no longer experimental (but still in alpha, with lots of updates and improvements coming in the next few weeks).

- Updated Component Testing intro: https://docs.cypress.io/guides/component-testing/introduction
- Changelog: https://docs.cypress.io/guides/references/changelog
- Migration guide: https://docs.cypress.io/guides/references/migration-guide#Component-Testing

We now have a dedicated component testing runner (which builds on top of the existing runner, but has some changes like not needing to launch the electron app to select a spec, and using a dev-server architecture instead of file:preprocessor, making it a (lot) faster.

As your your request, since we now have a component testing specific runner, we support [runner specific config](https://docs.cypress.io/guides/references/configuration#Runner-Specific-Overrides). You can specify `component` in `cypress.json` for component testing specific overrides. eg:

```json
{
  "testFiles": "cypress/integration/**/*.spec.js",
  "component": {
    "componentFolder": "src",
    "testFiles": "**/*.spec.ts"
  }
}
```

This will apply a different test glob for component tests (when launching component testing via `yarn cypress open-ct`. There is no way to actually *know* if a spec file is meant to be executed as a component testing or an e2e test, though, so you'll need to find some way to differentiate the two. You could do:

```json
{
  "integrationFiles": "**/__e2e__/*cy.ts",
  "component": {  
    "testFiles":  "**/__tests__/*.cy.tsx",
    "componentFolder": "src"
  }
}
``` 

Now you component tests can live next the component they test. 🎉 

If you find a better convention, please share! Let us know if you have any problems upgrading to Cypress 7.0. The [migration guide](https://docs.cypress.io/guides/references/migration-guide#Component-Testing) is kind of long, but the amount of code changes are fairly small, so it should not be too difficult.

We also noticed a huge increase in elapsed time in our CI after upgrade to 7.0.0.
I ran some CPU benchmarks against the latest versions. When testing with electron as browser, there's a large difference between 6.8.0 and 7.0.0. When testing with headless chrome, there's a difference starting from 6.7.1, but also a large increase in 7.0.0.

My [benchmark script](https://gist.github.com/kristianm/d2cd6cbf64e5dcab8853046b91b91214) was run against the [cypress kitchensink example repo](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress-example-kitchensink).
[See my results as comment in the same gist](https://gist.github.com/kristianm/d2cd6cbf64e5dcab8853046b91b91214#gistcomment-3695568).

If CPU usage has been correctly accounted in my tests, then there's a huge increase in CPU usage in 7.0.0 release, especially in sys space. Since the benchmarks were executed on my local laptop with multiple cores, the difference in real elapsed time is not as high as the increase in cpu usage. But in resource-limited environments such as CI containers, the real elapsed time will be affected even more.

As @Xdudu said, it's an expected behavior. Internally, should('not.be.empty') use jQuery's `is(':empty')`. And the result for `is(':empty')` against "length 0" jQuery object is `false`. Please check the code below:

```js
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.5.0.js"></script>
</head>
<body>
 
<script>
console.log($( "#doesnotexist" ).is(':empty')) // => false
</script>
 
</body>
</html>
```

### Workaround

Use `should('not.exist')` instead like `cy.get('DOESNOTEXIST').should('not.exist')`;

Internally, `cy.get()` uses jQuery engine. When your selector contains characters that are used in CSS, you need to add `\\` in front of that character. In your case, it should be `cy.get('nickname\\.\\.\\.1234')`

The confusion about the logs is because currently, there are two types of network logs:

* logs for XMLHttpRequest object creation (xhr) - these come from the cy.route and cy.server implementation
* logs for matched cy.intercept request (req)

So an XHR that hits a cy.intercept will log both. This is suboptimal UX, there is an issue open to track consolidating the two logs into one: https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/issues/14843

---

Because of the way XMLHttpRequests work, the `.status` property of a successful 200 response (cached and returned as the response to a 304 or not) will always be `200`. You can't get a `304` via the XHR API.

`cy.intercept` works on actual raw HTTP requests, not XMLHttpRequests, so it can get either a `200` response with a body or a `304` response with no body from the destination server.

There is no body with `304` responses, so that's why the response object is missing a body in your example.

We are working on improving the UI around this whole situation, it's still not as clear as it could be. Specific suggestions are welcome.

---

I think we can close this issue since this is known behavior. If there is a new bug with cy.intercept, feel free to open an issue.

Seems like it is trying to use the Jest type definition for the "describe" block. Please read our https://on.cypress.io/typescript documentation.

If you are using both Jest and Cypress in the same project, the TypeScript types registered globally by the two test runners can clash. For example, both Jest and Cypress provide the clashing types for the `describe` and `it` functions. Both Jest and Expect (bundled inside Cypress) provide the clashing types for the `expect` assertion, etc. There are two solutions to disentangle the types:

1. Configure a separate `tsconfig.json` for E2E tests. See our example [cypress-io/cypress-and-jest-typescript-example](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress-and-jest-typescript-example) repo.
2. Remove Cypress global variables by using NPM package [local-cypress](https://github.com/bahmutov/local-cypress). Read the blog post [How to Avoid Using Global Cypress Variables](https://glebbahmutov.com/blog/local-cypress/) for details.

@flotwig @jennifer-shehane I have 1 crucial use case to use `cy.wait('@alias.all')` is when using lazy loading React component. Full flow:
- User navigate to 1 specific path which is being lazily loaded
- The request pattern is `**/*.chunk.js` (intercept alias as `@chunks`)
- Cypress need to wait all requests under `@chunks` to finish to make sure the component is rendered in the page
- Then assert some expect statement

After a bunch of playing with it, I arrived at the following system for automatically bisecting, assuming we're looking for differences in Chrome/Electron CPU time. [This gist](https://gist.github.com/agg23/89138a4be6db5dcbce8ba163ac054020) contains the final run scripts.

This was run on an AWS `t2.xlarge` (this is important), configured in the following way:
```
wget https://dl.google.com/linux/direct/google-chrome-stable_current_amd64.deb
sudo apt install ./google-chrome-stable_current_amd64.deb
sudo apt install build-essential unzip

git clone https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress-example-kitchensink.git
cd cypress-example-kitchensink
yarn

cd ../
git clone https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress.git
```

The process was initiated via:
```
git bisect start 0399a6e58e226b860a41acf2847ee43adb8ad41e 73317218230319d45689bbad3ce46e7ab2312e18
git bisect run ./bisect.sh
```

considering 0399a6e58e226b860a41acf2847ee43adb8ad41e (tag 7.0.0) as known bad and 73317218230319d45689bbad3ce46e7ab2312e18 (tag 6.8.0) as known good.

This process turned up b52ac98a6944bc831221ccb730f89c6cc92a4573 as the first bad commit. This commit is notable as it both updates to a new major version of Electron (12.0, from 11.3.0) and a new major version of Node (14.16.0, from 12.18.3). However, it doesn't seem likely that upgrading Electron would change Chrome performance whatsoever.

Looking at the numbers, that does indeed seem to be the case, as Chrome numbers did not change significantly other than one run being significantly faster than the others. This also points to another potential problem. As seen in https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/issues/15779#issuecomment-815269145, both Chrome and Electron were noted to slow down with each version upgrade.

1. I speculate that Electron (the default for `cypress run`, which is what will be used in CI) has been slowed at least by the Electron upgrades, which is the primary cause of the visibility in #15779 and #15853. This problem is exacerbated on limited CI machines.
2. Chrome has a more niche slowdown, specifically correlated with strength of the machine. On ample resources, Chrome runs fine, but when constrained, the differences between 6.6, 6.7, 6.8, and 7.0 slow it down in some way.

**TLDR:**

I'm on board with this so long as you can prevent prettier from doing three things:

### 1. do not nest `.then()` on a newline. 

The `.then()` should be flattened to the same indention as the outer promise. example:

```js
// good
new Promise((resolve) => {

})
.then(...)
.then(...)
```

```js
// bad (the way prettier does this)
new Promise((resolve) => {

})
  .then(...)
  .then(...)
```

This leaves dangling `)}` that don't match the indentation for really **no good reason**.

### 2. do not force a single chainable `.then()` to be on the same line

It should accept either a single line or new line

```js
// good
new Promise((resolve) => {

})
.then(...)
```

```js
// bad (the way prettier does this)
new Promise((resolve) => { ... }).then(...)
```

Basically prettier nesting and rules surrounding when to force things into a single line is always bad, and should be left to the developer to decide when to insert the newline.

### 3. do not force multiple chainables to be multiline

```js
// good
Promise.resolve().tap().catch()
```

```js
// also good
Promise
.resolve()
.tap()
.catch()
```

```js
// bad (the way prettier does this)
Promise.resolve()
  .tap()
  .catch()
```

In addition, it means adding a single chainable call forces the calls to be across multiple lines.

As far as I'm aware - there is no way to force prettier to handle this via configuration, and I would accept a `patch-package` modification to get this in. Or alternatively, we modify the parser via the programmatic API to accommodate this.

### Edit

I found a less opinionated fork of prettier here: https://github.com/brodybits/prettierx

There is an option called: `--no-indent-chains` which is exactly what we want. We could borrow the implementation or perhaps just use `patch-package` to remove the offending `indent()` function calls.

**NOTE**
It is also available as a `plugin` of `prettier` via this: https://github.com/brodybits/prettier-plugin-x

### Edit 2

Could we not also use this? https://github.com/prettier/prettier-eslint 

This will run prettier first, and then we could run targeted eslint rules to change the formatting overrides.

@blakestoddard Thanks for opening a PR. The code looks solid (missing tests tho); however, I don't think that we can merge this feature.

[`cy.visit()`](https://on.cypress.io/visit)'s goal is to simulate a user visiting a web page in their browser, like via a bookmark or by clicking some hyperlink somewhere. That is why HTTP basic auth is supported by passing `auth` to `cy.visit` - real browsers support sending HTTP basic auth with a visit, so Cypress's API seeks to enable and match that behavior.

HTTP bearer token auth, on the other hand, is not (AFAIK) ever sent with a regular visit. The bearer token is always added later down the line by the JS code making the request.

With this in mind, it doesn't really make sense to add `bearer` to the `auth` property, since it's not something that makes sense to add to a visit.

Also, I am not totally sure, even after reading this PR and #4837, what a valid use case for this looks like. It seems like if the purpose is to send a request for a test with `bearer` auth, you should just use [`cy.request()`](https://on.cypress.io/request) or the `fetch` API.

----

That being said, there is a way to do this today with [`cy.intercept()`](https://on.cypress.io/intercept), if you decide that you really need to send `bearer` auth with a `cy.visit`:

```ts
cy.intercept('/url-to-visit', (req) => {
	// intercept the cy.visit and add auth header with bearer token
	req.headers['authorization'] = 'bearer <token...>'
})

// later...
cy.visit('/url-to-visit')
```

----

Closing this since it won't be merged. I'll post a link to this comment in the parent issue and close it too.

I am closing this issue since we won't be adding HTTP bearer auth to the `cy.visit` API at this time.

However, if you really need to send a bearer token with an HTTP request, there is a workaround: https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/pull/15596#issuecomment-818909685

Please read https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/pull/15596#issuecomment-818909685 for reasoning and workaround.

Hey Zach! Happy to expand a bit more on this.

For the use-case I have, I can't simulate OAuth/SSO because of some CORS restrictions in Cypress and in our app. The workaround is fetching a `bearer` token from an authentication service (which I do as a `Cyress.Command`) and then injecting that into the initial request so that it is authenticated (HTTP basic auth, the bearer token, cookie -- they're all valid methods of authentication). The issue I run into is that that app makes other external calls to, say, GraphQL that won't be authenticated without `bearer` token injection by Cypress (in regular operation they would have the cookie store, but I can't simulate it for Reasons), and if they're unauthenticated, the app gets into a bad state because effectively you're authenticated for the initial page-load but it can't fetch data client-side.

Using `cy.visit()` emulates that flow -- "visit this page with this set of authentication info and then force that in all of the child network requests too".

I would like to add that I've also encountered this bug and created a similar minimal repoduction (if needed).

`cy.route()` had an undocumented (but typed) `duration` property, but it was never part of `cy.intercept()`. You can read more about the history of this on this SO answer: https://stackoverflow.com/a/66356009/3474615

---

You could use `cy.intercept()` to manually construct timing information for a request. For example, if you want the total duration of a request and response cycle, you could do something like the following:

```js
let duration

cy.intercept('/something', (req) => {
	const requestReceivedAt = Date.now()
	req.on('response', (res) => {
		duration = Date.now() - requestReceivedAt
	})
}).as('getSomething')

// later...

cy.wait('@getSomething')
.then(() => {
	expect(duration).to.be.whatever
})
```

---

It would be nice to add a timing API for `cy.intercept()` so you don't have to manually measure this. We could add more detail than the old `duration` property allowed. A good template for this is the HAR 1.2 spec, which provides several timing statistics that you are probably used to seeing in the DevTools Network pane. From http://www.softwareishard.com/blog/har-12-spec/#timings :

> blocked [number, optional] - Time spent in a queue waiting for a network connection. Use -1 if the timing does not apply to the current request.
> dns [number, optional] - DNS resolution time. The time required to resolve a host name. Use -1 if the timing does not apply to the current request.
> connect [number, optional] - Time required to create TCP connection. Use -1 if the timing does not apply to the current request.
> send [number] - Time required to send HTTP request to the server.
> wait [number] - Waiting for a response from the server.
> receive [number] - Time required to read entire response from the server (or cache).
> ssl [number, optional] (new in 1.2) - Time required for SSL/TLS negotiation. If this field is defined then the time is also included in the connect field (to ensure backward compatibility with HAR 1.1). Use -1 if the timing does not apply to the current request.
> comment [string, optional] (new in 1.2) - A comment provided by the user or the application.

Cypress could expose all or some of these on the object yielded by `cy.wait()`.

Ok, here are my proposals. There are several options.

## Just don't clean up `<head>`

This is pretty similar to what Jest will do. If you modify `document.head`, it will be persisted between tests. Generally, cleaning up between tests is good, but this is an option.

I think we will still clean up `<body>` - this makes sense, since we want to mount a new component each test.

## Partial opt-out of cleaning up

We could provide some way to opt-out of specific clean up. In the example of `styled-components`, this is injected:

```
<style data-styled="active" data-styled-version="5.0.0">.qBWUh{margin-bottom:1rem;}</style>
```

A potential opt-out API might be something like this:

```js
const Line = styled.div`
  margin-bottom: 1rem
`

const SearchResults = (props) => (
  <Line>Stuff</Line>
)

mount(<SearchResults />, {
  persist: '[data-styled]'
})
```

Anything found via the `querySelector` syntax passed into `persist` could not be cleaned up. This would likely be confusing, though, since most people probably don't think about how `styled-components` work, and would have to make the connection before coming across the `persist` option.

## `<head>` opt-out

```js
mount(<SearchResults />, {
  reset: {
    head: true,
    body: false
  }
})
```

I guess we'd probably default to... `false`? Although it feels correct to clean up between tests, in practice it seems like most of the time this is not the desired behavior.

## Full opt-out

```js
mount(<SearchResults />, {

@Develliot @JochenDiekenbrock I am going to try to explain why it is failing.

Pardon my English if it is not too clear, English is not my first language.

In the component testing runner, we load a spec file once.
We then execute each it statement within the file.
When the component loads, the loader installs the styles for the component in a place of its choosing. 
Since before each test we cleanup the installed components and re-init the header for everything that has beed added during the test. If we did it after each test, we would not see anything in the renderings.

Come to our issue here: The styles added by `styled-components` are added in the zone of the DOM that is NUKED before each test. We have to figure out a way to leave these styles alone somehow.

The code for this is done in [cypress-io/cypress#16015](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/pull/16015), but has yet to be released.

We will no longer clean up `<head>` or `<body>`, except for things injected by Cypress. For example, you can inject a stylesheet like so:

```js
mount(<Foo />, {
  stylesheets: ['https://boostrap.com/styles.css']
})
```

We *do* clean up that stylesheet - this is expected, since it's part of the `mount` API, and of course we *do* clean up the mounted component in between each test. We will *not* clean up stylesheets injected from userland libraries, like `styled-components`, Emotion, etc. This should generally match the behavior most users will expect.

This solves the use cases presented here. If any others arise, we can just patch them as we go, but I can't think of any edge cases off the top of my head.

There are some ways you can mitigate the increased video size if necessary:

- You can decrease the compression of the video: https://docs.cypress.io/guides/guides/screenshots-and-videos#Video-encoding
- You can delete the video if a certain condition is met (like all the tests pass). This will skip compression. https://docs.cypress.io/api/plugins/after-spec-api#Delete-the-recorded-video-if-the-spec-passed
- You can configure the browser window size to a smaller size for smaller videos: https://docs.cypress.io/api/plugins/browser-launch-api#Set-screen-size-when-running-headless

```JSX
mount(<StyleSheetManager disableCSSOMInjection={true}>
  <ThemeProvider theme={theme}>
      <App />
  </ThemeProvider>
</StyleSheetManager>
)
```

"Switches to the slower text node-based CSS injection system for adding styles to the DOM. Useful for integrating with third party tools that haven't been upgraded to consume styles from the CSSOM APIs."

I figured out what to do, just in case you are still interested @hlb-schmidt or anyone else in the future:
Assuming you have correctly installed cypress and can run it headless:` yarn run cypress run` (or whichever way you run it, `npm` etc)

**1. You need an X-Server on the host.**

- On Linux, you already have and X Server running
- On Mac, On Mac OSX you can install XQuartz

**2. Enable X-forwarding on your Vagrant VM**

Just add this to your `Vagrantfile`
`config.ssh.forward_x11 = true`

**3. Ssh into the box without vagrant ssh**
We need to access the guest with `ssh` as opposed to the normal  `vagrant ssh`. Do do this:
run `$ vagrant ssh-config` on the host in your directory with the vagrant file

```
$ vagrant ssh-config
Host default
  HostName 127.0.0.1
  User ubuntu
  Port 2222
  UserKnownHostsFile /dev/null
  StrictHostKeyChecking no
  PasswordAuthentication no
  IdentityFile /Users/xxxx/work/.vagrant/private_key
  IdentitiesOnly yes
  LogLevel FATAL
  ForwardX11 yes
```
From this we have the details we need to ssh. The  `user`, the `HostName` the `Port` and the `IdentityFile`.

Now we can, from the host `ssh` into the guest and run the cypress test runner. 

We also need to add `-X` flag that tells `ssh` to use the X-forwarding.

Assuming my project runs in a directory called `project` in the home directory of my guest machine... Run this command from the host machine while your box in running.

`ssh vagrant@127.0.0.1 -X  -p 2222 -i  /Users/xxxx/work/.vagrant/private_key -t "cd /home/vagrant/project;  yarn run cypress open"`

Voila! the Test runner will run in your box and the GUI will display on your host machine.

Credits to [Gabor](https://code-maven.com/xforwarding-from-vagrant-box) and [Martin](https://coderwall.com/p/ozhfva/run-graphical-programs-within-vagrantboxes)

Bring your own webpack is exactly what I'm going for. Nextjs seems kind of unique in that they bundle and ship their own webpack implementation.

I made this PR: https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/pull/16108

Basically users need to have either `webpack@4` or `webpack@5` installed (and the relevant `html-webpack-plugin`). Those are listed as [`peerDependencies`](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/pull/16108/files#diff-e385749d8138fa9c2e7c04a2ad111a9ebb9e547525f6bb10f1e4fd5f1a8c8934R30-R31), with a range of 4-5. The other main change is to remove [`html-webpack-plugin`](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/pull/16108/files#diff-e385749d8138fa9c2e7c04a2ad111a9ebb9e547525f6bb10f1e4fd5f1a8c8934L14) from `dependencies`, so `@cypress/webpack-dev-server` won't try to install and use it's own one.

The only real downside here is we require quite a lot of `peerDependencies`.

- `webpack`
- `html-webpack-plugin`
- `@cypress/webpack-dev-server`

I don't think this really a major problem. Most templates will specify their `webpack` and `html-webpack-plugin`, which are installed to `node_modules`. Nextjs is the exception, with its inline webpack.

I think this solution is a little better in terms of long term maintainability. We are also working on a `yarn create cypress-tests` scaffolder - this would be the place to check for the existence of `next.config.js` and install the relevant `webpack` and `html-webpack-plugin` versions.

[Here is the offending line in Create React App](https://github.com/facebook/create-react-app/blob/master/packages/react-scripts/config/modules.js#L47). I tested this by moving my `support.ts` file into `src` and changing my `cypress.json` to say `"supportFile": "./src/support.ts"` and it worked.

Rendering of the Command Log surely slows down tests, especially if test takes a few minutes to run - as I understand adding more elements to the log slows down rendering of both log and page being tested - a design choice making this unavoidable.

The CYPRESS_NO_COMMAND_LOG=1 option is great to improve overall speed but does not help when tests fail as test recording does not contain essential information of what operations led to the error.

Indeed keepCommandLogSectionsClosed would help to replace CYPRESS_NO_COMMAND_LOG=1 option and performance improvement with Command Log is considerable as you know already, but it would still make post-analysis of a failed test more difficult.

Even if Command Log rendering would be implemented using a virtual table, it might not be fast enough to solve above performance concerns.

@NPC As part of Cypress’s [pricing](https://www.cypress.io/blog/2021/03/16/new-pricing-that-scales-seamlessly/), we included the ability to [cancel test runs when a test fails](https://on.cypress.io/smart-orchestration#Cancel-test-run-when-a-test-fails). This setting is accessible from the Dashboard for organizations starting at the [Business Plan](https://www.cypress.io/pricing/).

This offers a solution for those running tests using the Cypress Dashboard - and also ensures a parallelized run is cancelled so that all parallel running specs will also be cancelled to save time on the run.

**To get this feature, you will need to update to Cypress 6.8.0 and also be a member of an organization subscribed to a [Business Plan](https://www.cypress.io/pricing/).**

---

This feature was implemented with parallelized runs in the Dashboard in mind since this was the hardest use case to address. We had to build this feature specifically to continue to receive all of the tests in a cancelled run to ensure proper reporting. Now that we have a mechanism to cancel runs across these channels of communication, we can now consider a way to initiate cancelling test runs when a test fails from the Test Runner when not recording to the Dashboard. (Likely this would be implemented by some CLI flag or config specifying `cancelOnFailures: true)

**See [this issue](https://github.com/cypress-io/cypress/issues/518) for cancelling test runs when a test fails from the Test Runner when not recording to the Dashboard.**
